text: The thirÂ­ teenth century witnessed considerable and sustained inflation which potentially eroded the real value o f royal revenues and inevitably drove up expenditure (FigÃ¼re 1.7).2 7 Then, after a period o f economic stability and growth in the mid- thirteenth century, there was a gradual decline in agricultural output culminat- ing in a serious crisis during the early fourteenth century and the eventual collapse o f arable farming after the cataclysm o f the Black Death.2 8 These devel- opments made it increasingly obvious that escalating royal expenditure could not be met out of a domain-based fiscal system.

text: It is somewhat ironic that the increase in rescheduling o f royal debts under Henry VI arose not solely from a shortage of cash but from a desire to emulate the policies o f Henry V, who had equated good kingship with sound financial management: in a sense, the increase in reassignments was a mark o f the administrative integrity, rather than the financial disorder, that prevailed in the mid-fifteenth century Exchequer.5 5 To emphasize this point it m ay be helpful to examine two o f the most important areas o f royal spending in the later Middle Agesâ€” the repayment o f loans and the expenditure on warâ€” and demonstrate how the political and financial implications o f the royal debt changed from the time of Edward I to that of Henry VI.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Down to c.1340 the English crown depended for most o f its credit on large- scale loans provided by a series of Italian merchant banks.5 6 Although these loans were supposedly guaranteed against, and repaid from, the profits o f indirect (and more occasionally of direct) taxation, the scale o f royal borrowing was often out o f ali proportion to the real value o f the taxes, and the crown's refusal to keep faith with its foreign creditors contributed to the collapse o f several of the Italian firms.5 7 When these sources dried up in the middle o f the fourteenth century, the crown came to rely heavily on loans provided by English prelates, magnates and merchants.5 8 The Exchequer was quick to realize that members o f the domestic political elite could not be treated in the same arbitrary fashion and that the value o f loans wou!d therefore have to match the sources o f income against which they were guaranteed.

text: IV As has been shown, the switch from a domain-based fiscal system in the twelfth century to a tax-based one in the fourteenth reflected the monarchy's perception of the gradual shift in the nature and the exploitable resources o f the English economy.
text_raw:
IV
As has been shown, the switch from a domain-based fiscal system in the twelfth 
century to a tax-based one in the fourteenth reflected the monarchy's perception 
of the gradual shift in the nature and the exploitable resources o f the English 
economy.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: From the middle o f the fourteenth century, however, the structure of royal finance altered very little, and the tax system therefore failed to reflect the very dramatic changes that came about in the agricultural and urban economies and in the social and geographical distribution of wealth during the century and a half following the Black Death.

From the middle o f the fourteenth century, however, the structure of 
royal finance altered very little, and the tax system therefore failed to reflect the 
very dramatic changes that came about in the agricultural and urban economies 
and in the social and geographical distribution of wealth during the century and 
a half following the Black Death.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: The explanation for this failure is probably a political one: the devolution o f financial and political control to Parliament and the increasing tendency to delegate govemmental authority to the localities during the fourteenth century created an entrenched political elite whose inter- ests were best preserved by the maintenance o f the status quo.6 5 This trend certainly had important consequences for taxation.

text: In evaluating the development o f the fiscal state in Europe, the example of medieval England may be said to provide three important general themes which will recur in many o f the ensuing medieval and early modem case studies.
text_raw:
In evaluating the development o f the fiscal state in Europe, the example of 
medieval England may be said to provide three important general themes which 
will recur in many o f the ensuing medieval and early modem case studies.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Firstly, even very early monarchical states could create highly sophisticated and productive systems for raising revenue which not only reflected the political authority of the king but also tapped some of the most important sources of wealth in the society and economy Ã¶ver which he ruled.
text_raw:
Firstly, even very early monarchical states could create highly sophisticated and 
productive systems for raising revenue which not only reflected the political 
authority of the king but also tapped some of the most important sources of 
wealth in the society and economy Ã¶ver which he ruled.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Secondly, there was a strong tendency for precocious and successful tax systems to become ossified and increasingly to serve the interests not o f the state but o f its more powerful subjects.
text_raw:
Secondly, there was a 
strong tendency for precocious and successful tax systems to become ossified 
and increasingly to serve the interests not o f the state but o f its more powerful 
subjects.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Thirdly, the medieval idea that a ruler had a right to dispose o f his resources as he willed continued even after the shift away from the exploitation o f prerogatives to the negotiation o f tÃ¢xes, thus slowing down the emergence of a genuine system o f public finance based on a declared budget, a permanent mechanism allowing for public accountability and, perhaps above ali, the estab- lishment of a public debt.

Thirdly, the medieval idea that a ruler had a right to dispose o f his 
resources as he willed continued even after the shift away from the exploitation 
o f prerogatives to the negotiation o f tÃ¢xes, thus slowing down the emergence of 
a genuine system o f public finance based on a declared budget, a permanent

lishment of a public debt.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: The absence of these principles and practices from English medieval state finance do not prevent us from identifying England as one o f the most sophisticated and successful fiscal regimes known in Europe between the late tvvelfth and the early fifteenth centuries.

The absence of these principles and practices from 
English medieval state finance do not prevent us from identifying England as 
one o f the most sophisticated and successful fiscal regimes known in Europe 
between the late tvvelfth and the early fifteenth centuries.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: But the failure o f the Yorkist and early Tudor monarchs to effect a fiscal revolution on anything like the same scale as that mounted betvveen the late thirteenth and mid-fourteenth centuries inevitably raises serious questions about the success of their much- vaunted reforms in the central financial administration.

But the failure o f the 
Yorkist and early Tudor monarchs to effect a fiscal revolution on anything like 
the same scale as that mounted betvveen the late thirteenth and mid-fourteenth 
centuries inevitably raises serious questions about the success of their much- 
vaunted reforms in the central financial administration.
